title: What is a binary search tree (BST) — a binary tree where left child < parent < right child; this makes searching fast.
shortTitle: What is a Binary Search Tree (BST)?

s1_definition.profdef: A binary search tree is a binary tree that maintains an ordering invariant: for every node, all values in its left subtree are smaller than the node's value and all values in its right subtree are larger. This invariant lets search, insert, and delete run in time proportional to the tree's height, which is logarithmic when the tree is balanced. An inorder traversal of a BST visits the values in sorted ascending order.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India arranges account balances on a special noticeboard shaped like a tree. Every balance smaller than the one in your hand hangs on the left branch, and every larger balance hangs on the right. To find a particular balance you start at the top and at each step go left if your target is smaller or right if it is larger. You never look at the whole board — you eliminate half the possibilities at every step, so you reach the answer in just a few hops.
s1_definition.oneliner: A BST keeps smaller values on the left and larger on the right, so each comparison halves the search.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A binary search tree is a binary tree that maintains an ordering invariant: for every node, all values in its left subtree are smaller than the node's value and all values in its right subtree are larger. This invariant lets search, insert, and delete run in time proportional to the tree's height, which is logarithmic when the tree is balanced. An inorder traversal of a BST visits the values in sorted ascending order.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India arranges account balances on a special noticeboard shaped like a tree. Every balance smaller than the one in your hand hangs on the left branch, and every larger balance hangs on the right. To find a particular balance you start at the top and at each step go left if your target is smaller or right if it is larger. You never look at the whole board — you eliminate half the possibilities at every step, so you reach the answer in just a few hops.

**One line to remember:** A BST keeps smaller values on the left and larger on the right, so each comparison halves the search.

sections.s2_technical:
The ordering invariant is what distinguishes a BST from a plain binary tree. Because the left subtree is always smaller and the right subtree always larger, you can search by comparison instead of by scanning.

To search, you start at the root and compare. For example `if (target.compareTo(node.value) < 0) go left; else if (target.compareTo(node.value) > 0) go right; else found`. Using compareTo keeps it correct for BigDecimal balances. Each comparison discards half the remaining tree, so in a balanced BST with n nodes you reach any value in about log base two of n steps. Insert follows the same path until it finds an empty spot and links the new node there. Delete is the trickiest: a leaf is simply removed, a node with one child is replaced by that child, and a node with two children is replaced by its inorder successor, the smallest value in its right subtree.

Inorder traversal of a BST produces sorted output, which is a beautiful property: visiting left, node, right always yields ascending values. This makes a BST a natural ordered map or ordered set.

A senior-level point is balance. If you insert already-sorted data into a naive BST, it degenerates into a straight line, essentially a linked list, and search drops to linear time. Self-balancing variants fix this: AVL trees keep strict height balance, and red-black trees keep an approximate balance with cheaper updates. Java's TreeMap and TreeSet are red-black trees, guaranteeing logarithmic operations and sorted iteration. In banking, this is exactly what you want for range queries like finding all accounts with balances between two amounts.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India maintains a live index of account balances and must answer the question "does an account with exactly this balance exist?" extremely quickly, and also list balances in sorted order for reports. A plain list would force a full scan for each lookup. A binary search tree keeps the balances ordered so each lookup eliminates half the tree, giving fast search, and an inorder traversal prints them already sorted.

Problem 2 — New balances are inserted throughout the day as accounts change. The tree must accept inserts while keeping the smaller-left, larger-right invariant so that future searches stay fast. Insertion walks the same comparison path and links the new value at the correct empty spot.

In our mini-project we build a `BalanceBST` storing BigDecimal balances, with insert, contains, and an inorder listing. The demo inserts several of the bank's balances, searches for a present and an absent value, and prints the balances in sorted order.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: insert balances 250000, 1000000, 50000, 300000, 75000, then search for 300000 and 999999.

Step 1: Insert 250000. The tree is empty, so 250000 becomes the root.

Step 2: Insert 1000000. Compare with root 250000; it is larger, so it goes to the right child of the root.

Step 3: Insert 50000. Compare with 250000; it is smaller, so it goes to the left child of the root.

Step 4: Insert 300000. Compare with 250000, larger, go right to 1000000. Compare with 1000000, smaller, so it becomes the left child of 1000000.

Step 5: Insert 75000. Compare with 250000, smaller, go left to 50000. Compare with 50000, larger, so it becomes the right child of 50000.

Step 6: Inorder traversal visits left, node, right throughout, producing the sorted order 50000, 75000, 250000, 300000, 1000000.

Step 7: Search 300000. From root 250000 go right to 1000000, then left to 300000, found. Search 999999. From 250000 go right to 1000000, then left to 300000, then right which is null, not found.

sections.s6_takeaway:
A binary search tree is a binary tree that maintains an ordering rule: for every node, everything in its left subtree is smaller and everything in its right subtree is larger. That single invariant is what makes searching fast, because at each node I compare my target with the node's value and move left or right, discarding half of the remaining tree on every step. In a balanced tree that gives logarithmic search, insert, and delete.

The way I describe it from my banking work is as a live balance index at the National Bank of India. We need to quickly check whether an account with a given balance exists and also list balances in sorted order for reports. By keeping balances in a binary search tree, each lookup eliminates half the tree, and an inorder traversal visiting left, node, right conveniently produces the balances already sorted ascending. I always use compareTo on BigDecimal so the ordering is correct for money.

I walk through the operations concretely. Search and insert both follow the comparison path from the root. Delete is the one that needs care: a leaf is simply removed, a node with one child is replaced by that child, and a node with two children is replaced by its inorder successor, which is the smallest value in its right subtree.

The senior-level point I stress is balance. If I insert already-sorted data into a naive BST it degenerates into a straight line and search falls back to linear time. That is why in production I rely on self-balancing trees. Java's TreeMap and TreeSet are red-black trees that guarantee logarithmic operations and sorted iteration, which is exactly what I want for range queries like finding every account whose balance falls between two amounts. So I understand the plain BST deeply, but in real systems I reach for the balanced variant.
